text: Camp Nou. Eighty-eighth minute. Barcelona are winning three–one.
And they're still going out of the Champions League. To get through, they need three more goals — in about seven minutes, including stoppage time.
In the entire history of the competition, no team had ever come back from four goals down after a first leg.
This is the story of the night it happened anyway. The six–one. The comeback that made no sense.
We'll start in Paris, with the defeat that seemed to end everything. Then the plan Luis Enrique built to do the impossible.
Then the seven minutes that made the night famous — and finally, the uncomfortable truth about what happened after.
Part one. The humiliation.
On Valentine's Day twenty seventeen, Barça went to Paris for the first leg of the round of sixteen. They were thrashed.
Ángel Di María scored twice. Julian Draxler and Edinson Cavani added the others. Four–nil.
It wasn't just the score. Barça were overrun. Paris Saint-Germain pressed them, out-ran them and out-played them. Messi, Suárez and Neymar barely touched the ball in dangerous areas.
The next morning, the reaction was brutal. People said that this great Barça team was finished. Bookmakers made a comeback almost impossible.
And a couple of weeks later, Luis Enrique announced that he would leave the club at the end of the season.
For most people, the second leg was just a formality. A chance to say goodbye with some dignity.
Part two. The plan.
Luis Enrique decided that if Barça were going out, they would go out attacking. He picked a team with just three defenders at the back.
Wide players pushed right up the pitch. Midfielders pushed forward. The idea was to play almost the whole game in Paris Saint-Germain's half.
And when Barça lost the ball, they had to win it back immediately — because there was hardly anyone behind them to defend.
It was a huge risk. One counter-attack, one goal for Paris, and Barça would need even more. But at four–nil down, the risk was the only option.
Part three. The perfect start.
It started almost perfectly. In the third minute, Luis Suárez forced the ball over the line with his head from close range. One–nil.
Just before half-time, Andrés Iniesta's flick across the box was turned into his own net by the defender Layvin Kurzawa. Two–nil.
Five minutes into the second half, Neymar went down in the box. Penalty. Messi scored it. Three–nil.
Three–nil, with forty minutes left. One more goal and the tie would be level. The Camp Nou was shaking.
Part four. The goal that killed it.
And then, just after the hour, Edinson Cavani scored. Three–one.
That one goal changed the mathematics completely. Paris now had an away goal. That meant Barça didn't need one more goal anymore. They needed three.
The stadium went quiet. For the next twenty-five minutes, Barça pushed and pushed. Chances came and went.
When the clock reached eighty-eight minutes, it was still three–one. Most people in the stadium had accepted it. Some had already started to leave.
Part five. Seven minutes.
Eighty-eighth minute. Free-kick, just outside the area. Neymar curls it over the wall and into the top corner. Four–one.
Ninety-first minute. Suárez goes down in the box. Penalty. Messi, the usual taker, hands the ball to Neymar. He scores. Five–one.
Now it's five–one. Five–five on aggregate. But Paris have more away goals. Barça still need one more. And there are only a few seconds left.
Ninety-fifth minute. One last free-kick, deep in Barça's half. Everyone goes forward. Even Marc-André ter Stegen, the goalkeeper, is in the Paris box.
The ball comes to Neymar on the left side of the area. He doesn't panic. He lifts a soft, chipped pass over the defence.
And arriving at the far post, stretching out his right foot, is Sergi Roberto — a player who had come through La Masia.
Six–one. Barcelona are through.
Three goals in about seven minutes. The first team in Champions League history to overturn a four-goal deficit from the first leg.
The noise in the stadium was so intense that sensors at a scientific observatory in the city were reported to have picked up the vibrations.
Luis Enrique, who had been calm all night, sprinted onto the pitch. Fans in the stands were crying. Many of the people who had left early heard it on the radio, outside the stadium.
Part six. Neymar's night.
Messi scored a penalty. Suárez scored and won a penalty. But in the final minutes, this was Neymar's night: the free-kick, the penalty, and the assist.
It was the best performance of his time at Barça. It made him feel, maybe for the first time, that he could be the main star — not Messi's sidekick.
And that feeling would have consequences.
Part seven. The hangover.

Here's the uncomfortable truth. A month later, in the quarter-finals, Barça went to Turin and lost three–nil to Juventus. In the return leg at the Camp Nou, they couldn't score at all. No miracle this time.
At the end of the season, Luis Enrique left, as he had announced.
And that summer, Neymar left too — to Paris Saint-Germain, the very team he had destroyed. They paid his two-hundred-and-twenty-two-million-euro release clause.
And as we've explained in our episode on Barça's finances, the way the club spent that money helped dig the hole it is still climbing out of today.
That's what makes the six–one so strange to remember. It was the most incredible night in the club's modern history.
But it was also a kind of ending. The front three of Messi, Suárez and Neymar would never be this good together again.
For Sergi Roberto, though — a La Masia boy who scored the goal of his life in the ninety-fifth minute — it will always just be the night of the comeback. And for millions of culers, too.
Is the six–one the greatest comeback in Barça history? Or is there another night you'd put above it? Tell me in the comments.
